If this is not the case for some face _F_, we can add new demands parallel to each edge of _E(F_) of demand weight \(\epsilon>0\), and increasing the capacity of each edge in _E(F_) by \(\epsilon\), and extend _x_ by routing along these single-edge paths. This does not introduce any new crossings. Now, it suffices to show the nested supports property holds for _x_.

By using parallelizations, we may assume all paths are edge-disjoint. Consider two distinct faces _F_<sub>1</sub>_,F_<sub>2</sub>. To simplify the notation, for _i_=1,2 let _x<sup>i</sup>=x<sup>F<sub>i</sub></sup>_ and let \(G_i=G[\mathrm{supp}(x^i)]=G[\mathrm{supp}(x^i)\cup E(F_i)]\). For _i_=1,2, we will use the notation <o>_i_</o> to mean the number in {1,2}\\{_i_}. First, we prove that for each \(i\in\{1,2\}\), _G<sub>i</sub>_ is contained in a single face of \(G_\overline{i}\). We will deal with the stellated supports at the end.

Observe that for \(i\in\{1,2\}\) and any \(P\in\mathrm{supp}(x^i)\), the other face \(F_\overline{i}\) is contained in either Ext(_C(P_)) or Int(_C(P_)).

**Claim A.3.** _Let_ \(i\in\{1,2\}\).

• _If the face F<sub>i</sub> is contained in_ Int(_C(P_)) _for_ \(P\in\mathrm{supp}(x^\overline{i})\)_, then every path_ \(Q\in\mathrm{supp}(x^i)\) _is contained in_ Int(_C(P_))_, and hence G<sub>i</sub> is contained in_ Int(_C(P_)).<tbc>

• _If the face F<sub>i</sub> is contained in_ Ext(_C(P_)) _for_ \(P\in\mathrm{supp}(x^\overline{i})\)_, then every path_ \(Q\in\mathrm{supp}(x^i)\) _is contained in_ Ext(_C(P_))_, and hence G<sub>i</sub> is contained in_ Ext(_C(P_)).

_Proof._ Suppose that _F<sub>i</sub>_ is contained in Int(_C(P_)) for \(P\in\mathrm{supp}(x^\overline{i})\). The cycle _C(Q_) has an edge (namely, its demand edge) that lies in int(_C(P_)). If it leaves Int(_C(P_)), it must cross the cycle _C(P_), which means it must cross the path _P_. This contradicts the earlier claim. The case for Ext(_C(P_)) is similar.

We say _F<sub>i</sub>_ is _universally exterior_ if _F<sub>i</sub>_ is contained in Ext(_C(P_)) for all \(P\in\mathrm{supp}(x^\overline{i})\). Note that if _F<sub>i</sub>_ is universally exterior, then by Theorem A.3, _G<sub>i</sub>_ is contained in Ext(_C(P_)) for all \(P\in\mathrm{supp}(x^\overline{i})\).

**Claim A.4.** _Either F_<sub>1</sub> _is universally exterior or F_<sub>2</sub> _is universally exterior._

_Proof._ There are two cases.

Case 1: there exists \(P_1\in\mathrm{supp}(x^1)\) such that _F_<sub>2</sub> is contained in Int(_C(P_<sub>1</sub>)). Now, consider \(P_2\in\mathrm{supp}(x^2)\). Then by Theorem A.3, we have that _P_<sub>2</sub> is contained in Int(_C(P_<sub>1</sub>)), and consequently _P_<sub>1</sub> is contained in Ext(_C(P_<sub>2</sub>)). Furthermore, this implies that _F_<sub>1</sub> is contained in Ext(_C(P_<sub>2</sub>)), since if _F_<sub>1</sub> were contained in Int(_C(P_<sub>2</sub>)), then Theorem A.3 would imply that _P_<sub>1</sub> is contained in Int(_C(P_<sub>2</sub>)). Hence _F_<sub>1</sub> is universally exterior.

Case 2: there does not exist \(P_1\in\mathrm{supp}(x^1)\) such that _F_<sub>2</sub> is contained in Int(_C(P_<sub>1</sub>)). Then _F_<sub>2</sub> is contained in Ext(_C(P_<sub>1</sub>)) for all \(P_1\in\mathrm{supp}(x^{H_{F_1}})\), and _F_<sub>2</sub> is universally exterior.

**Claim A.5.** _If F<sub>i</sub> is universally exterior, then the other support graph_ \(G_\overline{i}\) _is entirely contained within a single face of G<sub>i</sub> (note that this face is possibly bounded or unbounded)._

_Proof._ Let \(F_i^*\) be the face of _G<sub>i</sub>_ that contains \(F_\overline{i}\). We will show that for all \(P\in\mathrm{supp}(x^\overline{i})\), the cycle _C(P_) is contained in \(F_i^*\), which proves the claim.

Let _h_ be the (embedded) demand edge routed by _P_. Certainly the demand _h_ is contained in the interior of \(F_i^*\) since it is embedded in the interior of \(F_\overline{i}\). Now, if _C(P_) ever leaves \(F_i^*\), then there exists a node _v_ that is incident with four distinct edges that alternate in clockwise order between _C(P_) and supp(_x<sup>i</sup>_). Say listed in clockwise order these are _e_<sub>1</sub>_,e_<sub>2</sub>_,e_<sub>3</sub>_,e_<sub>4</sub>, where \(e_1,e_3\in C(P)\) and \(e_2,e_4\in\mathrm{supp}(x^i)\). However, since _C(P_) is a simple cycle, then at least one of _e_<sub>2</sub>_,e_<sub>4</sub> must enter int(_C(P_)), which contradicts that _F<sub>i</sub>_ is universally exterior.

Now, suppose without loss of generality that _F_<sub>1</sub> is universally exterior, and thus _G_<sub>2</sub> is contained in a single face \(F_1^*\) of _G_<sub>1</sub>. If _F_<sub>2</sub> is also universally exterior, then we are done. So suppose not. Then there exists \(P_1\in\mathrm{supp}(x^1)\) such that _F_<sub>2</sub> is contained in Int(_C(P_<sub>1</sub>)), and hence by Theorem A.3 we have that _G_<sub>2</sub> is contained in Int(_C(P_<sub>1</sub>)). Therefore the face \(F_1^*\) of _G_<sub>1</sub> that contains _G_<sub>2</sub> must be a bounded face. It then follows that _G_<sub>1</sub> must be contained within the unbounded face of _G_<sub>2</sub>.

Thus we have proven that for each _i_, _G<sub>i</sub>_ is contained in a single face of \(G_\overline{i}\). For each _i_, let _S<sub>i</sub>_ be the star graph added to _G<sub>i</sub>_ to obtain _G_\[_x,F<sub>i</sub>_\] (so that _G_\[_x,F<sub>i</sub>_\]=_G<sub>i</sub>+S<sub>i</sub>_.

Now fix an \(i\in\{1,2\}\). Let \(F_i^*\) be the face of _G<sub>i</sub>_ that contains \(G_\overline{i}\). First, observe that \(G[x,F_\overline{i}]=G_\overline{i}+S_\overline{i}\) is still contained in that same face of _G<sub>i</sub>_, since the star \(S_\overline{i}\) is added into the open interior of \(F_\overline{i}\) and its embedding is completely disjoint from \(G_\overline{i}\).

So \(G[x,F_\overline{i}]\) is contained in a single face \(F_i^*\) of _G<sub>i</sub>_. The only way that \(G[x,F_\overline{i}]\) is not contained in a single face of _G<sub>i</sub>+S<sub>i</sub>=G_\[_x,F<sub>i</sub>_\] is if adding the star _S<sub>i</sub>_ divides \(F_i^*\) into multiple faces. However, for this to happen we would need that \(F_i^*=F_i\) (recall that _F<sub>i</sub>_ is a face of _G<sub>i</sub>_, since we assumed that \(E(F_i)\subseteq\mathrm{supp}(x^{F_i})\)). However, it cannot be the case that \(F_i^*=F_i\), since the leaves added to \(F_\overline{i}\) are not contained in _F<sub>i</sub>_ but are in \(G_\overline{i}\).

Thus \(G[x,F_\overline{i}]\) is contained in a single face of _G_\[_x,F<sub>i</sub>_\]. By a symmetric argument we have that _G_\[_x,F<sub>i</sub>_\] is contained in a single face of \(G[x,F_\overline{i}]\) This concludes the proof.

## B Randomized Rounding for Maximization

In this section, we prove Theorem 4.4.

_Proof._ Let \(\nu,\gamma\in(0,1)\) be constants, sufficiently small so that \(\frac{1-\gamma}{1+\nu}\ge 1-\epsilon\) (for example, \(\nu=\gamma=\epsilon^2\) suffices).

Let P be the set of support paths of _f_. We first proceed with some assumptions about the input data. By scaling _w_, we may assume \(w(h)\le 1\) for each \(h\in E(H)\) and _w_<sub>max</sub>=1. Finally, observe that we may assume \(f(P)<\frac{1}{\mathrm{log}^2n}\) for each \(P\in\mathcal{P}\). Otherwise we can decompose _f=f_<sub>1</sub>+_f_<sub>2</sub> where _f_<sub>2</sub>(_P_) is some multiple of \(\frac{1}{\mathrm{log}^2n}\) and \(f_1(P)<\frac{1}{\mathrm{log}^2n}\) (for each _P_, let _k<sub>P</sub>_ be the maximum positive integer such that \(f(P)-\frac{k_P}{\mathrm{log}^2n}\ge 0\) and define \(f_2(P)=\frac{k_P}{\mathrm{log}^2n}\) ). Then we can apply the lemma to _f_<sub>1</sub> to obtain \(\hat{f}_1\), and \(\hat{f}=\hat{f}_1+f_2\) satisfies the desired properties for the original flow _f_.

Proceeding under the above assumptions, define an integral flow \(\bar{f}\) by independently assigning each \(\hat{f}(P)\) to 1 with probability \(\mathrm{log}^2n\cdot f(P)\in[0,1)\) and otherwise assigning it 0. We use the following Chernoff bounds.

**Lemma B.1** (Chernoff Bounds)**.** _Let X_<sub>1</sub>_,...,X<sub>k</sub> be mutually independent random variables where_ \(X_i\in[0,1]\)_. Let_ \(X=\sum_iX_i\) _and let_ \(\mu_\mathrm{max}\ge\mathbb{E}\left[X\right]\ge\mu_\mathrm{min}\)_. The following inequalities hold:_

1. _For any_ \(\delta\ge 1\) _we have_<tbc>

<tbc>\(\mathrm{Pr}\left[X\ge(1+\delta)\mu_\mathrm{max}\right]\le\mathrm{exp}(-\delta\mu_\mathrm{max}/3).\)<tbc>

_2._ _For any_ \(\delta\le 1\) _we have_<tbc>

<tbc>\(\mathrm{Pr}\left[X\le(1-\delta)\mu_\mathrm{min}\right]\le\mathrm{exp}(-\delta^2\mu_\mathrm{min}/2).\)<tbc>

<tbc>How much does \(\bar{f}\) congest an edge _e_? We have that \(\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{P\unknown e}\bar{f}(P)\right]=\mathrm{log}^2n\cdot\sum_{P\unknown v}f(P)\le\mathrm{log}^2n\) since _f_ is feasible. Let B_<sub>e</sub>_ be the (bad) event that \(\sum_{P\unknown e}f(P)\ge(1+\nu)\mathrm{log}^2n\). Setting \(\mu_\mathrm{max}=\mathrm{log}^2n\) and \(\delta=\nu\) in Theorem B.1, we obtain:<tbc>

\(\mathrm{Pr}\left[\mathcal{B}_v\right]\le\mathrm{exp}(-\nu\mathrm{log}^2n)=n^{-\nu\mathrm{log}n}.\)

<tbc>What value does \(\bar{f}\) achieve? We have that \(\mathbb{E}\left[w(f)\right]=\sum_h\sum_{P\in\mathcal{P}_h}w(P)\mathbb{E}\left[\bar{f}(P)\right]=\mathrm{log}^2n\cdot\sum_h\sum_{P\in\mathcal{P}_h}w(h)f(P)=\mathrm{log}^2n\cdot w(f)\). Let B_<sub>w</sub>_ be the (bad) event that \(w(f')\le(1-\gamma)\mathrm{log}^2n\cdot w(f)\). Setting \(\mu_\mathrm{min}=\mathrm{log}^2n\cdot w(f)\) and \(\delta=\epsilon\) in Theorem B.1, we obtain:

\(\mathrm{Pr}\left[w(f')\le(1-\gamma)\mathrm{log}^2n\cdot w(f)\right]\le\mathrm{exp}(-\gamma^2\mathrm{log}^2n\cdot w(f)/2)=n^{-\gamma^2w(f)/2}\le n^{-\gamma^2/2}\)

where the last inequality follows from \(w(f)\ge w_\mathrm{max}=1\).

Thus by the union bound, the probability that one of the events \((\mathcal{B}_v:v\in E(G))\) or B_<sub>w</sub>_ occurs is at most \(\frac{n^2}{n^{\upsilon logn}}+\frac{1}{n^{\gamma^2/2}}\), which converges to 0. Thus with high probability, we obtain an outcome \(f'\) that avoids all of these bad events.

Now let \(\hat{f}=\frac{1}{(1+\nu)\mathrm{log}^2n}f'\). Since \(f'\) avoids B_<sub>e</sub>_ for each edge _e_, \(\hat{f}\) is feasible. Additionally, since \(f'\) avoids B_<sub>w</sub>_, we have that \(w(\hat{f})=\frac{1}{(1+\nu)}w(f')\ge\frac{(1-\gamma)}{(1+\nu)}w(f)\ge(1+\epsilon)w(f)\).

## C NP-Completeness of Fractional Uncrossed Multiflow

In this section we prove the NP-completeness of deciding the existence of a fractional uncrossed flow satisfying all demands. The proof is reminiscent of a reduction by Middendorf and Pfeiffer \[23\], for the node-disjoint paths problem when _G+H_ is planar. We remark that this shows NP-completeness even for leaf instances of multiflows. We refer to a fractional uncrossed flow which satisfies all demands as a _solution_.

In the first subsection, we show the problem is in NP (which is not necessarily obvious, given that uncrossed fractional multiflow is not a linear program). In the next subsection, we introduce the key gadgets which are used in the proof of NP-hardness, and in the subsection after we present the main proof of NP-hardness.

## C.1 Polynomial-Sized Solutions

Adding uncrossed-ness to the constraints of a multiflow problem means it is no longer a linear program, and it is not necessarily obvious that we should expect uncrossed solutions that are polynomial in the size of the input (i.e. in terms of |_V|,|E(G_)|,|_E(H_)|, and the bit-size of _u,d_).

We give a brief argument for why polynomial-sized solutions exist. Let _f_ be a feasible uncrossed (fractional) multiflow for a maximization or congestion instance. Consider a single commodity \(h=(s,t)\in E(H)\), and consider the single-commodity uncrossed multiflow _f<sup>h</sup>_, obtained by restricting _f_ to _h_. Let _P_<sub>1</sub>_,...,P<sub>k</sub>_ be the clockwise ordering of the support paths about _s_. Each sector (i.e. the region bounded between consecutive paths in this ordering) contains some face _F_ of _G_ that is not contained in any other sector. Hence there are at most _O_(|_V_|) sectors, and thus _O_(|_V_|) paths. Thus over all commodities the set of support paths P<sup>∗</sup> is at most _O_(|_V_||_E(H_)|). To obtain values of _f(P_) that have polynomial bit-size, we can set up restricted versions of the maximization/congestion linear programs that only have variables for \(P\in\mathcal{P}^*\). By standard linear programming theory there exists a solution for these problems that has polynomial bit-size, and any solution for these LPs is uncrossed as they draw support paths only from P<sup>∗</sup>.

A consequence of this argument is that the problem of determine whether (_G,H,u,d_) has a feasible (fractional) solution that is uncrossed is in NP, as promised by Theorem 1.7. Given a polynomial-sized candidate solution, it is straightforward to check that each pair of support paths is uncrossed and that the solution is feasible in polynomial time.

**Theorem C.6.** _It is NP-hard to determine whether there is an embedding of G in which_ (_G,H_) _has a fractional uncrossed multiflow._

**Claim C.7.** (_G,H_) _has an uncrossed solution (in the original embedding) if and only if the new instance has an uncrossed solution._

_Proof._ It is straightforward to verify that if (_G,H_) has an uncrossed solution, then so does the new instance. We show the converse, that if the new instance has an uncrossed solution, so too does (_G,H_). Consider an arbitrary uncrossed solution _f_ for the new instance. ## D Colouring Uncrossed String Graphs

In this section, we prove the following result.

**Theorem D.1.** _Let U be an uncrossed string graph arising from a realization with at most k paths on any edge. Then_ \(\chi(U)=O(k^2log|E(U)|)\).

The following is the key lemma.

**Lemma D.2.** _Let U be an uncrossed string graph with a load k realization_ (_G,_P)_. Then U is the union of O(k_<sup>2</sup>log|_E(U_)|) _planar graphs._

_Proof._ We generate a random subgraph _H_=(_S,F_) of _U_ as follows. First, we select random subset \(S\subseteq\mathcal{P}\) by drawing each \(P\in\mathcal{P}\) independently and uniformly at random with probability \(q=\frac{1}{k}\). Now, for each \(e\in E(G)\) such that \(|S\cap\mathcal{P}_e|=2\) exactly, we add to _F_ an edge between the two members of \(S\cap\mathcal{P}_e\). Note that _H_ is planar.

Let \(PP'\in E(U)\), and consider the event that \(PP'\in E(H)\). This event happens if there exists some _e_ with \(P,P'\in\mathcal{P}_e\) where \(P\in S\), \(P'\in S\), and no other path in P_<sub>e</sub>_ is in _S_. Clearly there is at least one _e_ such that \(P,P'\in\mathcal{P}_e\), and we lower bound the probability that \(PP'\) is included due to this particular edge. Then,<tbc>

\(Pr\left[PP'\in E(H)\right]\ge q\cdot q\cdot(1-q)^{k-2}\ge\frac{1}{k^2}\left(1-\frac{1}{k}\right)^{k-2}\ge\frac{1}{ek^2},\)

where the last inequality follows from the fact that \((1-1/x)^{x-2}\ge 1/e\) for all _x\>_1.

We repeat this process _C_=2_ek_<sup>2</sup>log|_E(U_)| times, independently, obtaining random subgraphs _H_<sub>1</sub>_,...,H<sub>C</sub>_ of _U_. For \(PP'\in E(U)\), let \(A_{PP^\prime}\) be the event that for all \(i\in[C]\), \(PP'\notin E(H_i)\). Then,

\(Pr\left[A_{PP^\prime}\right]\le\left(1-\frac{1}{ek^2}\right)^{2ek^2log|E(U)|}\le\left(\frac{1}{e}\right)^{2log|E(U)|}=|E(U)|^{-2},\)

where the second inequality follows from the fact that \((1-1/x)^x\le 1/e\) for _x\>_1.

Let _A_ be the event that there exists \(PP'\in E(U)\) such that for all \(i\in[C]\), \(PP'\notin E(H_i)\). That is, there exists \(PP'\in E(U)\) such that \(A_{PP^\prime}\) holds. By a basic union bound, \(Pr\left[A\right]\le|E(U)|\cdot|E(U)|^{-2}<1\). So there is an outcome in which _A_ does not hold. In this outcome, _U_ is covered by the graphs _H_<sub>1</sub>_,...,H<sub>C</sub>_. Hence _U_ is the sum of _C_ planar graphs.

From this, Theorem D.1 follows easily.

_Proof of Theorem D.1._ We show that _U_ is _O(k_<sup>2</sup>log|_E(U_)|)-degenerate, from which the result follows. As the property assumed in the theorem statement is hereditary (i.e. closed under node deletion), it suffices to show that _U_ contains a node with at most _O(k_<sup>2</sup>log|_E(U_)|) neighbours.

By Theorem D.2, _U_ is the sum of _O(k_<sup>2</sup>log|_E(U_)|) planar graphs. Each planar graph contributes at most 3|_V(U_)| parallel edge classes, so it follows that _E(U_) contains at most _O(k_<sup>2</sup>|_V(U_)|log|_E(U_)|) parallel edge classes. Hence it contains a node with at most _O(k_<sup>2</sup>log|_E(U_)|) neighbours.
